title: Ultrasonic Testing for Steel Mills | UT Inspection (US)
description: On-site ultrasonic testing for US steel and metals plants: ladle hooks, crane girders, shafts, gearboxes, caster frames, shells. Send your list for a quote.
h1: Ultrasonic Testing for Steel Mills and Primary Metals Plants in the United States
html:
Atlantis NDT carries out ultrasonic testing (UT) at US steel mills, foundries, forges and aluminum plants: crack detection in ladle hooks and trunnions, crane structure welds, roll necks and shafts, gearbox housings and caster frames, plus thickness surveys on furnace shells, ductwork and water piping. Technicians are mobilized to the plant for the agreed outage or running-line scope. Send the equipment list and request a UT inspection quote.

Where ultrasonic testing fits in a steel plant

A steel plant makes components fail in ways that few other industries do. Parts are heated and cooled repeatedly, loaded with hundreds of tons of molten metal, and exposed to scale, water and dust. The consequence of failure is severe, so hooks, trunnions, crane structures and drive shafts are examined on a schedule. Ultrasonic testing is the method that sees inside those heavy sections. A sound pulse enters the steel, and a crack, inclusion or shrinkage cavity reflects part of it back. A hook shank forged from a thick bar can have a defect centimeters below the surface that no surface method would ever reveal.

UT is also the thickness tool: shells that run hot, ducts carrying corrosive gas, cooling water piping and baghouse housings thin gradually, and a survey on a grid shows where. The sibling pages on magnetic particle inspection for steel and penetrant testing for steel deal with surface cracks. UT answers a different question: what is inside, and how much wall is left.

Equipment and components in scope

  • Ladle hooks, trunnions and lifting beams. Forged hook bodies and trunnion pins carry the full ladle load. Angle-beam and straight-beam scans look for cracks that start in the shank, the saddle and at changes of section.
  • Overhead crane structure. Girder and end-truck welds, runway beams, bridge and trolley frames, and wheel and axle assemblies on process cranes that handle hot metal.
  • Roll necks, drive shafts and spindles. Fatigue cracks grow at keyways, couplings seats and fillets. Straight-beam scanning along the shaft from the end finds transverse cracks long before they cause a break.
  • Gearboxes and mill stands. Housing welds, large gear and pinion blanks, and shafts. Our scope for rolls is shaft and neck work on site; barrel inspection of work rolls happens in a dedicated roll shop and is outside this page.
  • Continuous caster segments and frames. Segment frames, support rolls, shafts and bearing housings, examined at planned caster outages.
  • Furnace structures and vessels. Shells, tilting trunnion rings, support steel and water-cooled hood panels. Heat gradient and scale complicate the scan, and the technician adjusts for them.
  • Utility systems. Gas mains, oxygen and nitrogen lines, cooling water headers, and dust collection ductwork, surveyed for remaining wall.

Cranes, hooks and the rules that apply

Cranes that carry molten metal are the highest-consequence equipment in the plant. OSHA 29 CFR 1910.179 sets inspection duties for overhead and gantry cranes in general industry, including frequent and periodic inspections, and ASME B30.2 is the industry standard those requirements are drawn from. Hooks follow ASME B30.10. Crane welding is covered by AWS D14.1, the specification for welding industrial and mill cranes, and its acceptance criteria are commonly applied to UT of crane welds. The crane owner and its qualified person decide whether a crane remains in service; our report supplies the NDT data they need.

For examination methods we rely on ASME Section V, Article 4 for weld examination, ASTM E164 for contact testing of weldments, ASTM A388 for ultrasonic examination of steel forgings, ASTM E114 for straight-beam testing, and ASTM E797 for thickness. Where a procedure must be built from scratch, technical procedure development can supply it. All work is done by technicians qualified under the Atlantis written practice based on ASNT SNT-TC-1A, Level II performing and interpreting, with an ASNT Level III approving procedures and reviewing reports. The code article for welds is ASME Section V Article 4 explained.

Heat, scale and access: technique at a steel plant

The conditions drive the technique more than the code does.

  • Surface temperature. Standard couplants and probe wedges are limited to modest temperatures. Surfaces warmer than that need high-temperature couplant, probes made for heat and short contact times, or a cool-down window. We measure surface temperature first and record it.
  • Scale and rough surfaces. Mill scale and rolled finish scatter sound. We grind a contact area and keep notes on where it is, so repeat readings line up.
  • Thick sections. Large forgings attenuate sound and require lower frequency probes and careful gain. A reference block of the same material and similar size is used for sensitivity.
  • Geometry. Hooks, trunnions and rolls have curved faces, so we use contoured wedges or probes and sketch each scan path.
  • Calibration. The instrument and probe are calibrated before the job, again at the work area, and checked at intervals and at the end, as the procedure states.

What UT finds in steel plant equipment, and where it falls short

Method choice for mill equipment
ComponentBest examined withNote
Ladle hook shankUT and MTUT for internal flaws, MT for surface cracks
Crane girder weldUT and MTMT on toes, UT for lack of fusion and buried flaws
Roll neck or shaftUT from end or diameterMT when removed from the stand
Furnace shell, duct, pipeUT thickness surveyGrid on a CML map
Aluminum or stainless partUT inside, PT on surfaceMT does not apply

UT does not describe everything. Coarse grain in heavy castings scatters sound, cracks nearly parallel to the beam can be missed, and a hot or scaly surface may prevent a valid reading. We tell you at quote stage when a component will limit the examination. Atlantis does not perform radiography in the United States, and techniques other than UT, MT and PT are not offered in this service.

Mini-mills, forges, foundries and aluminum plants

Not every primary metals plant is an integrated mill. Electric arc furnace mini-mills concentrate on furnace shells and roofs, scrap handling cranes, casting machines and rolling stands. Forging plants run presses and manipulators whose rams, columns and tie rods take enormous cyclic loads, and their own dies and tooling blocks crack from the inside. Foundries and aluminum smelters rely on cranes, pot shells, crucible supports and large rotating machinery. The inspection list differs, but the method is the same: an internal examination of heavy sections and thickness surveys on parts that lose metal. We prepare a plan for each plant's own equipment rather than a generic checklist, using the maker's inspection recommendations where they exist and flagging components that deserve a closer look based on service history. Where a mill keeps its own inspection history, we compare new readings against earlier ones so that a slow trend, such as a gearbox housing weld that has grown a little with each outage, is visible and not buried in one report.

Planning outages and plant rules

Steel plants run around the clock, and inspection often waits for a scheduled outage on a line, a caster or a furnace. We plan with the maintenance team: lock-out and tag-out under 29 CFR 1910.147, confined-space permits under 1910.146 for vessels and ducts, hot work permits, fall protection for crane runways, and escorts in areas with molten metal or energized equipment. Contractors must complete the plant's safety orientation, and we ask for the requirements when you contact us. Expect to supply or arrange scaffolds, lifts and clean power. We agree dates with your planner and do not quote arrival times.

What the report contains

The report names each component and location, the procedure and revision, the instrument and probe serial numbers, the calibration blocks and checks, the surface temperature and condition, and the technician and level. Thickness work includes the grid map with every reading and the minimum found. Hook, shaft and weld work lists each indication with position, depth, length and amplitude, and states accept or reject against the criterion named in the order. Sketches show scan paths and probe positions. A Level III reviews and signs. For weld-specific work, see ultrasonic weld inspection, and for forgings and castings such as hooks, pinions and housings, see ultrasonic testing of castings and forgings.

What to send for a quote

  • Equipment list with drawings, weld maps or photographs, and previous inspection records.
  • Material, thickness and surface temperature while running or after cooldown.
  • Acceptance code or owner specification, and the crane rating or maker data for hooks and trunnions.
  • Access: scaffold, lifts, confined spaces, permits and who supplies them.
  • Plant address, safety orientation requirements and the outage window.

Training your plant technicians

Steel plants often prefer in-house readers for routine thickness checks. Atlantis delivers UT Level 1 training and UT Level 2 training, and its ultrasonic testing simulator gives practice on flaw response. The plant, as employer, certifies its staff, and a written practice governs. Related reading: the ultrasonic testing guide, the national UT page and manufacturing NDT training.

faq.q: Can you inspect ladle hooks and trunnions with UT?
faq.a: Yes. We scan forged hook shanks, saddles and trunnion pins with straight-beam and angle-beam probes to find internal cracks and inclusions, usually combined with magnetic particle testing for surface cracks. The report gives each indication with position and size, and the crane owner decides on repair or retirement.

faq.q: Does OSHA require UT of overhead cranes?
faq.a: OSHA 29 CFR 1910.179 requires frequent and periodic crane inspections but does not specify UT. The crane's maker, ASME B30.2 and the owner's program decide whether NDT is needed. We provide the examination data that the qualified person uses.

faq.q: Can you test while the equipment is hot?
faq.a: Within limits. We measure surface temperature first and use high-temperature couplant and suitable probes where the procedure allows. Above those limits the part must cool or we schedule the work in the outage. Surface condition and temperature are recorded in the report.

faq.q: How do you find shaft cracks without removing the shaft?
faq.a: Straight-beam scanning from the end face or a clean section of the diameter detects transverse fatigue cracks that start at keyways and shoulders. Access, shaft length and coupling parts affect coverage, and we explain the limits at quote stage.

faq.q: Can UT measure wall thickness on hot gas ducts and furnace shells?
faq.a: Yes. We survey on a grid with a thickness gauge and record each reading and the minimum found, using high-temperature couplant when the surface is warm. Remaining life or repair decisions are for your engineer based on the data.

faq.q: Are you able to inspect work rolls?
faq.a: We examine roll necks, shafts and journals on site. Detailed barrel inspection of work and backup rolls is done in specialist roll shops and is not offered here. We will tell you which parts of the roll we can cover.

faq.q: What does a steel plant need to give you to quote?
faq.a: An equipment list with drawings or photographs, material and thickness, the acceptance criteria, access and permit arrangements, plant safety orientation requirements and the outage window. We reply within one business day, and a short list is enough to begin.

faq.q: Who decides if a cracked hook goes back into service?
faq.a: The crane owner and its qualified person, working with the maker's guidance and ASME B30 requirements. Atlantis reports the indications against the named acceptance criteria; it does not decide fitness for service.

faq.q: Do you do radiography at steel mills?
faq.a: No. Atlantis does not perform radiography in the United States because it is a licensed activity. Owners who need it hire a licensed firm. Ultrasonic testing is often chosen for volumetric checks of welds and forgings, and we can review radiographs as an ASNT Level III service.
